subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF NATION-WIDE SYSTEM

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF NATION-WIDE SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be in keeping with the practice which has been developed under the order for motions if I were to make a very brief and very informal statement at this time. We are today celebrating the anniversary of the birthday of this country, the linking of the four older provinces which at that time were united in one bond of determination to maintain their identity and independence, and to prevent absorption by the country to the south.
At that time communications were very limited. There was a telegraph system and a railway, but to the west there were no communications unless by smoke signals or messengers who used canoes. Then British Columbia joined confederation, and telegraph lines, railway lines and finally telephones were established. We could communicate back and forth in a fraction of a moment, and we could travel across this continent in a short time.
Today it has been made possible for us to see each other from one end of this continent to the other. Those who are living on the far west coast, beyond the Rocky mountains, can look over those hills and see how the rest of us in Canada live. We in the east can watch the industrial development of the various provinces. All this has been
made possible by the inauguration of a national television system, which has been established and is now in operation, extending from Sydney in Nova Scotia to Victoria in British Columbia, and shortly to be extended to Newfoundland.
I thought it fitting that this should be put on the record at this moment. The national program started at 4.30, just as we opened this sitting of parliament. I want to pay tribute to the engineers whose scientific abilities made possible this achievement in so far as plans and development are concerned. I also want to pay tribute to the various telephone companies who have financed this undertaking. I also want to pay tribute to the officers and staff of the C.B.C. whose imagination and courage have made possible this national system which we inaugurated some 15 minutes ago.

I share with him the hope that the extension to Newfoundland, without which it will not be complete, will soon be celebrated also.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INABILITY OF CANADA TO OBTAIN U.S. NUCLEAR WEAPONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED INABILITY OF CANADA TO OBTAIN U.S. NUCLEAR WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 25 the Leader of the Opposition asked me the following question:
-whether the Canadian government has made representations to the United States government

Inquiries of the Ministry concerning amendments to the United States atomic energy act, approved by the Senate in Washington on Monday, which would prevent Canada from obtaining United States nuclear weapons of any kind, and would make it illegal for the United States even to supply the information to enable Canada to design such weapons for use by our navy, army or air force?
I am bound to give a somewhat extended answer and I would ask you, sir, to blame the Leader of the Opposition for asking such a question rather than myself for the length of the answer.
I can assure the Leader of the Opposition that we have followed closely the discussions in the United States congress of the amendments to the United States atomic energy act. The house will appreciate that certain restraint has had to be exercised in discussing the legislation of another country while it is under review by the legislature of that country. The United States government is being kept fully aware of possible Canadian military requirements, and we anticipate that we would experience little difficulty because of the amendments under consideration in making any future arrangements with the United States government in the military application of atomic energy which may be necessary for our joint defence.
However, the Leader of the Opposition's question concerned a situation last week in which the United States congress was considering amendments proposed by the two United States houses to amendments proposed by the United States executive to an act which is already amended from the form in which it was originally conceived. I am sure the house will understand, therefore, that it would be inadvisable for me to comment in any detail at this stage on what has been a very complicated amending process.
I would, however, like to add a further comment on the implication of the question which has been asked. There is a suggestion in the question, it seems to me, that the process of amending the United States atomic energy act which is going on has in some sense made more restrictive the provisions of that act. I can with assurance tell the house that this is the exact opposite of the intent of the United States administration, as indicated in the hearings which have taken place over some months. Late last October, following discussions with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, the President of the United States indicated that he would request congress to amend the atomic energy act in order to permit close and fruitful collaboration in this field between the United States and other friendly countries. Again, in his message on the state of the union early this year, the President of the United States emphasized the necessity that congress enact

legislation to enable the United States to exchange appropriate scientific and technical information with friendly countries.
There have been a number of other statements by senior United States spokesmen which echo the view that the amendments were intended to liberalize existing United States atomic energy legislation. Many features of the act as it existed before the recent amending process remain unchanged. Even under the earlier provisions of the act it has been possible to meet Canadian requirements as they have developed.
At this stage it is impossible to be certain of all the implications of the amended act for Canada, or indeed for any other interested country. After the new act becomes effective there will follow a period when important interpretations have to be made of its terms in the light of specific requirements. Certainly the amendments would seem to provide somewhat more latitude for co-operation between the United States and friendly countries than was provided in the United States law preceding the amendments.
It is for this reason that the Canadian government anticipates that future Canadian defence needs, in so far as this area of cooperation with the United States is concerned, will be served just as in the past by the necessary degree of United States cooperation in this field that has been possible under existing United States legislation.
I have dealt with the general aspects of the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition. He has raised as well two particular points. So far as the first of these is concerned, it is not my understanding that the amendments to the United States atomic energy act in so far as they concern the supply of nuclear weapons to other countries affect in any way the provisions of the atomic energy act of 1954.
As to the final part of his question about supply and design information concerning atomic weapons, I should like to point out that the United States atomic energy act as amended will make provision for the supplying of United States restricted data necessary for the development of defence plans, the training of personnel in the employment of defence against atomic weapons, the evaluation of the capabilities of potential enemies in the employment of atomic weapons, and the development of compatible delivery systems for atomic weapons.
The implications of the revised United States atomic energy act for the Canadian defence program perhaps fall within the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of National Defence. I apologize for the length of the answer, but I could not possibly have done better.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO RETURN TO THE HOUSE OF MINISTER OF LABOUR
speechtext:
The Minister of Labour has
various duties, and I think most fair-minded members of the house will agree that since his appointment he has done an excellent job as minister.

The house resumed, from Monday, June 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Robichaud.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind hon. members of the first part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gloucester, because I wish to address my remarks now particularly to that part of the amendment. It asks the house to regret "that the government has failed, despite the measure announced on Friday by the Prime Minister, to avert the five-week shut-down in the Nova Scotia coal mines." It is quite obvious, sir, that this measure has failed to avert a shut-down.
The measure announced by the Prime Minister, welcome though it was-and I hasten to say that any expedient that could be justified at all would be welcomed by us
1798	HOUSE OF
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines on this side of the house in order to keep these miners at work-is after all only an expedient, and it is very hard to see why it would not have been just as easy for the government to take this action two weeks earlier and avert a shut-down altogether. After all, as I understand the statement of the Prime Minister, all the government is proposing to do is to pay the carrying charges on the stockpile of coal over and above the normal stockpile. If that would be a good thing to do at the end of June, it is very hard to understand why it would not be an equally good thing to do at the beginning of June, and it is very hard to understand why the government left this matter to the very last moment, because as was pointed out last night, and I do not intend to repeat it, the government had plenty of warning of what was coming.
The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan), who made the only speech on the government side deserving of any serious consideration, is obviously a good lawyer. He is the kind of lawyer one would engage to defend one if one had been guilty of murder, because I never heard a better attempt to make black appear white than the effort made by the hon. gentleman last evening. He talked about Liberal neglect and betrayal of the coal industry. He talked about that in the face of the indubitable fact that never during the Liberal regime were
9,000	miners thrown out of work at any one time, as has happened since the Tories came into office. He talked with total disregard of the fact that subventions, which have been in operation since 1928, were a Liberal expedient. He told us a fairy tale about Angus Macdonald, when the fact, of course, is that Angus Macdonald was a member of the government at the time the royal commission was established which recommended mechanization, one of the most serious efforts yet made to make the coal industry efficient and economically sound.
He also said that the present government had started the policy of having coal used in government buildings. I assume he was ignorant of the truth which is, of course, that that policy was in operation under the previous government. He talked about the power program instituted by Mr. Harris and Mr. Lesage, as so many Tories do, as if it had been instituted by the present government. He talked about the efforts of the present government to get an overseas market, and completely ignored the fact that the only successful effort in this regard was that made by the previous administration in arranging exports to the United Kingdom. He also talked about the market being protected in


Ontario and Quebec, in the face of the fact that that market is being lost more and more every day.
Even this belated action of paying the carrying charges on the stockpile is nothing new. It is true that it is a new expedient applied to the coal mines, but it is precisely the same policy as was applied two years ago by the Liberal government under the leadership of Mr. C. D. Howe with respect to the carryover of wheat. We cannot help but be flattered that, in order to meet an emergency, the present government should once again have to follow a precedent instituted by a Liberal government.
Since this is only an expedient, since this paying of carrying charges to the end of the year is going to solve absolutely nothing, it does seem to me that when the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys rises to speak he should tell us what is going to happen at the end of December. What is going to happen to the coal industry in 1959? The problem is still going to be there. The Prime Minister did indicate in a vague sort of way that there was some prospect of selling about 4 million tons. I think the minister should be precise and tell us just what there is to this prospect. What markets are in sight?
He should also tell us if there is an agreement already in force with Dosco, and he should lay the agreement on the table so we can see what is in it. He should also tell us whether Dosco has given any assurance that in the period beyond the end of this year collieries will not be closed, because there is a strong suspicion that it is the intention of the company to close collieries.
Now, sir, we had at least three members on the government side of the house last night quoting the statement made by Mr. St. Laurent at Fredericton something over a year ago. What did Mr. St. Laurent say? He said that he would not advocate any substantial increase in coal production. He said also there should not be any ghost towns created in the coal fields. In other words, what he was saying was that the policy that was applied to the gold mines so successfully by the previous administration, and which is being continued by this administration, should be applied to the coal mines. I say that no public man with any sense of responsibility would have promised a substantial increase in coal production in 1957. Hon. gentlemen opposite, not expecting to win an election and blinded by a vision-the vision of office -were ready to promise anything.
Here is what they did with that statement by Mr. St. Laurent. I have here a full-page advertisement from the Halifax Mail-Star

which is headed, "The Coal Industry; Action Today or Regret Tomorrow." It reads in part:
If coal production is not increased the services of some 4,000 of the 11,000 mine workers presently employed in the Nova Scotia coal industry will not be required.
This is a quotation from the Gordon commission. Then there is the quotation from Mr. St. Laurent, to which I have referred, and a quotation from Mr. Stanfield, the premier of Nova Scotia:
The Prime Minister, as a matter of policy, has set his face against the expansion of the coal industry in Nova Scotia . . . And on no issue is there greater disagreement than our stand on coal policy and the position taken by the Liberal party.
Hon. gentlemen had better not applaud too quickly.
In these statements above, the people of Nova Scotia may read for themselves and judge for themselves who has the best interests of Nova Scotia at heart.
Your Progressive Conservative candidates are in favour of a coal policy that will increase coal production! Do a good turn for Nova Scotia-turn out and vote Conservative on June 10.
What has happened since? Coal production has declined by 10 per cent up to this time, and the mines are closing. Obviously production is going to decline a great deal more than 10 per cent in the next five weeks.
You hope so.

Obviously production is going to decline, since there is going to be no production at all. The mines are going to be closed. What policy has the government for dealing with the coal industry, and for the future of the coal industry? The minister of northern affairs, speaking for the government, talked about a big steel mill some time in the future, some time within the next 40 years. The minister of northern affairs, with that long-range vision of his, was going to give us a steel mill in Nova Scotia.
But what do we really hear about the steel mill? We hear from Dosco that it is not in Nova Scotia they propose to build a steel mill. Dosco is proposing a steel mill in the greater Montreal area. What is the government going to do? Where is that policy of decentralization of the Tory resolutions drawn up at Moncton, on which they sold their policies a year ago? Where is the decentralization of industry? Apparently the decentralization of the steel industry is to be away from Cape Breton to Montreal.
There is no one on this side of the house who would not want to see a steel mill in Montreal. I do not believe there is any doubt that there will be a steel mill in Montreal. But it does seem extraordinary that this government, which got the votes of the
1, 1958	1799
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines people of Nova Scotia by telling them that the Conservatives were going to bring about decentralization of industry, are now sitting idly by while Dosco appears to be proposing to transfer its main operations from Cape Breton to the St. Lawrence.
It is not only in the coal industry, sir, that things have been happening in Nova Scotia. Mr. Henry Hicks gave a statement to the press on June 11, and this is what he said. This statement relates more particularly, of course, to the second part of our motion, which I will not take the time to read, the part referring to the government backing away from the decentralization of industry. This is what Mr. Hicks had to say:
In the past few months we have seen the closing down of several important and useful industries in Nova Scotia, most notably Consumers Cordage in Dartmouth, The Canadian Canners processing plant at Middleton, Moirs box mill at Bedford and the Wolfe Hat and Cap plant at Stewiacke. Even more recently, the announcement has been made of the probable closing of the Hamilton Biscuit Company at Pictou.
In addition to this, a disturbing number of business firms in Nova Scotia have gone bankrupt and made assignments in the past few months. The figures for 1957 were running three times as high as the figures for the previous two years. While the closing of these firms has come in for a good deal of public attention, I am suggesting that the public may not be fully aware of the lay-offs in other industries throughout the province. Some of them are known-the Halifax Shipyards Limited; Eastern Car plant at Trenton; Point Edward naval base-but there are others, lesser in numbers individually, but collectively involving many of our people.
While it is of course true that the Canadian economy is passing through a period of recession, there are definite signs to indicate that we in Nova Scotia are perhaps being affected more adversely than any other areas of Canada. For example, dominion bureau of statistics figures indicate that the housing industry in Canada is experiencing a substantial improvement for this year, but as was pointed out in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of June 4 in an article headlined "Home Building Booming, but not in Maritimes", we in this province are unfortunately not sharing in this improvement. Indeed all maritime provinces are substantially behind last year in home building figures.
Now, sir, in New Brunswick the decline in employment is evident in the collieries at Minto; in the closing down of the base metal mine in the Bathurst area; the closing of the textile mill at Milltown; the threat to the sugar refinery at Saint John, and if that goes the public has been told that Ganong's at St. Stephen may have to close.
Finally, sir, last night the minister of northern affairs gave us encouragement by telling us that the federally subsidized Beechwood power was being exported to the United States. This is happening at a time when the pleas of the government of Newfoundland for assistance in power development in that province are rebuffed by this

vision.
It does seem to me, sir, that already I have given enough evidence to show that whatever the government's intention may be the facts are-and it is the facts at which we have to look and the facts by which we have to judge -that in the past 12 months there has been a decline in economic activity in the maritime provinces even greater than the decline in other parts of Canada. There has not been any sign whatever of this policy of decentralization of industry about which so much was made before the June election, and even before the election of last March. As the vision fades before the harsh, clear light of reality, of another period of Tory hard times, the people of the maritimes-
Oh, oh.

I suggest hon. gentlemen just stop and listen-the people of the maritimes will regret the Tory discovery of the maritimes and their own discovery of the Tory party. I say that if things go on the way they are going at present in the maritime provinces, it will not be very long before people there are looking back to the golden age of Liberal neglect in the St. Laurent-Howe era, when the population increased; when income increased; when there was virtually full employment; when equalization multiplied by seven times the yield of direct taxes; when transfer payments from the federal government in Nova Scotia increased 9 times, in Prince Edward Island 11 times, and in New Brunswick 20 times, while they increased only 6 times in Ontario.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the
member of the government representing the province of Nova Scotia, I think perhaps I should intervene in this debate for a few moments. There is nothing much more to be said from this side of the house than was said yesterday in those four very able speeches that were delivered by the Nova Scotia members in opposition to this proposal which has been made. Despite the caterwauling and sarcasm of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down, I will tell him that he has never heard finer speeches made by four freshman members of the house at any time in all the years he has been sitting here.
It also was particularly appropriate, Mr. Speaker, that two of those speeches should be made by men who worked in the pits. I refer to the hon. member for


Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir). The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria suffered an accident resulting in a broken back. I think this house and this country will take the judgment of these men on the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia before they will take-no matter how respectable and how honourable the members may be-that pf an ex-fisheries inspector from Nova Scotia and an expatriate college professor from Winnipeg, particularly when the expatriate college professor has a schooner but has to get the William Carson to get him back to Newfoundland. If he is as much at a loss in navigating that schooner as he was in making that speech last night, he certainly needs a chart and compass to get him back on course again.
It was an amazing speech, Mr. Speaker. It had no beginning and it certainly had no end. It slithered something like a water snake, twisting and turning, without logic and without reason. When it ended there was nothing more said by it than there was at the beginning.
This is one of the great motions of want of confidence in the House of Commons, one of the six motions to go into supply when the substantial omissions of the government are brought to the attention of the house. If this is all the opposition could arraign this government on, then certainly the record of the government is very good indeed.
What are the facts of this matter? In the first place I should like to say this. I should like to pay tribute to the men who have been operating in the mines of Nova Scotia during these years, who have worked hard and have increased the daily production per man, which fact, together with mechanization, has resulted in the surplus which we have today. The men have gone for over four years without an increase in wages and without a new contract. They deserve full credit for the tremendous achievement which has been made in the development of coal in the Nova Scotia mines.
I should like to pay tribute to the leadership of the union, those leaders who came here and made their representations to the government. We heard the Prime Minister refer to them in the house the other afternoon. I am not going further except to say that it is a tribute to Canadian labour when you have men of that calibre representing a large union such as the U.M.W., which was referred to on this occasion.
It is true that there is overproduction at the moment. There seems to be a great deal of misunderstanding about this matter. I heard it suggested over on the other side of

the house yesterday-I do not think this was intended seriously-that this stockpile itself could not be sold during the coming year, that there were not orders enough to make that possible. The truth of the matter is that the company is selling more coal than was sold before. The truth of the matter is that there are orders for over 4 million tons of coal. The truth of the matter is that with the help of this government and with the-
Then why are they shutting down?

Wait a moment and I will
tell you. As I was saying, with the leadership of the company and the aggressive management and the co-operation of this government in subventions, they have sold over 350,000 tons of coal to new customers within the last two months, customers that were never found before. My hon. friend spoke about markets being lost in Ontario. That is the greatest poppycock I have ever heard. Markets have been developed in Ontario. That is why we increased the subventions. They are being developed rapidly in the province of Ontario. During the winter months and during this spring a stockpile developed there. The stockpile now is probably about 1,400,000 tons of coal.
There was also an election.

Yes, there was an election.
That is really the reason we have this motion today, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members opposite took the maritime provinces for granted so long that they thought the maritimers were helots, and that all they had to do was pull the string and they would vote Grit. But they finally woke up and had intelligence enough to vote Conservative, and hon. gentlemen opposite have not yet got over the shock. The maritimers ceased being taken for granted. That is a mistake the Liberals still make, in assuming that they will continue to vote for them.
As I was saying when I was interrupted, the stockpile is roughly 1,400,000 tons. There are orders for 4,600,000 tons of coal and orders are still coming in. Many of these orders are for green coal from the mine. You cannot translate the coal from the stockpile into the orders as they get them. Only a proportion can go. It is going to take months, perhaps into the winter, perhaps even into next spring before the whole stockpile is liquidated; and liquidated it will be, because the company will see to it that it moves out and, as I have said, the orders are recurring and multiplying.
What was the situation? We were told that we did not avert a lay-off of five weeks.

Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines We did not have an opportunity to avert a lay-off of five weeks. We were not consulted about a lay-off of five weeks. The company told us that a lay-off of five weeks was necessary for the efficient and economical management of the company's properties. We are not in a position to dictate to the company what it should do. The company went on to say that if that five-week lay-off, which was necessary, were not continuous but were spaced over the period of the next two or three months in various pits at different times, tied into the vacation period and so on, its impact-as serious as it is, of course- would be much less than if it were one that came with full force and was carried on consecutively through all the pits in the province. But the company did say that having inaugurated that lay-off of five weeks which they felt, from the standpoint of business efficiency and management, was necessary, it also would have to extend the lay-offs much further unless government assistance was forthcoming.
Assistance was discussed last week and the week before and various other weeks. The company proposed that one way in which it might be done would be to assist in the carrying charges of the surplus stockpile over and above the normal stockpile, of which of course they have had figures throughout the year. Those estimates were made. They were confirmed by the dominion coal board. We agreed and the government of Canada, in co-operation with the province of Nova Scotia, assumed the difference between the normal stockpile carry-over as estimated at the end of this year and the stockpile we estimate is going to be there. We take the interest, the stockpiling and the insurance and pay these expenses instead of having them paid by the company.
The company still has to raise the money. The company still is risking its capital. The company still has the coal to dispose of. These are the obligations of the company. It is a joint undertaking whereby the company advances the money and carries on the mine. We agreed to assume the cost of the additional burden over and above the normal to the end of this year. The province agrees to accept part of the cost.
Much has been said about this being paltry and about the way it has been done, but I want to say that the union officials who were here expressed tremendous satisfaction at the way in which this government had acted. There have been many quotations from the papers yesterday and today, most of them rumours and a dialectical display of a coup here and a coup there, but I want to refer to a statement appearing in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of yesterday,
1802	HOUSE OF
Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines which quoted Mr. Delaney, the union deputy board member who was here on Friday, as saying that there would have been, of course, much greater loss if this government had not acted at the request of the union, and that the federal government action was the fastest taken by any government in his experience.
We are supposed to be too slow; we are supposed to have been too late, but here is the national board member of the U.M.W., with all his experience in dealing with governments throughout the years, saying that the action we took was the fastest that has ever been taken. Where is all the specious poppycock we heard yesterday from the other side of the house? This government deserves tremendous gratitude for having done what it did. It has the endorsation of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, one of Nova Scotia's large newspapers; it has the endorsation of the Cape Breton paper; it has the endorsation of other large daily papers in the province; it has the endorsation of 95 per cent of all the weekly press in the province; it has the endorsation of the provincial government and has the endorsation of the united mine workers of America. The only thing it lacks is the support of the hon. members who spoke this afternoon and the few for whom they were speaking. I will take the support we have for our position and for the action which this government has taken.
This is not the first thing we have done for the coal industry. We increased subventions last year. In particular we increased subventions last fall for the mine at Springhill in order to keep that mine operating until it was eventually closed, not for lack of financial support but because of the physical situation which developed when the mine was temporarily closed until the seams were brought back to parallel. We increased subventions to other mines so the coal could be brought to other territories, and we increased subventions three weeks ago in order to allow
150,000	or 200,000 tons of coal to be moved into the Belleville area in Ontario. Now we have again increased subventions. Mind you, this should be made clear. This money is not being paid out to the company as such; it will probably not all be paid out this year. This money will be paid out in the form of subventions as the coal moves from the pit stockpile, and it probably will not all be moved and therefore the subventions will not all have been paid out until some time next year.
There has been some talk of corporations. I have no particular brief for this corporation, but I think it has done reasonably well in maintaining employment and in paying out millions upon millions-more millions of


dollars than have been paid out before-in producing coal and continuing to carry the burden, as the corporation is still carrying the burden, and spending money to keep going. It has to pay out all this money itself. It is a lot to do, and it is something which has not been done before.
The hon. member must certainly have been hard put to find an analogy for what his government did for the coal industry when he compared this action with what Right Hon. C. D. Howe did for wheat three years ago.
It is the same thing.

Is that the best comparison of what his government had done for coal? It is true that the former Liberal government under Mackenzie King in the early days of the twenties brought in coal subventions, but they were inadequate. They were not sufficient to keep the industry going. It was under the government of R. B. Bennett, when Gordon Harrington was premier of Nova Scotia, that subventions were increased materially so the economy of the Nova Scotia mining communities was restored and the mines operated for another 20 years. After those subventions were established, costs and freight rates increased until we reached another stage and we were losing our markets. What did the former Liberal government do in order to assist the Nova Scotia coal industry in those days? What did that government do during the last few years?
Hon. members pointed out yesterday afternoon the difficulties of the various mines, that this mine had closed down and another mine was closing down, and that thousands of men would be out of work.
One mine definitely closed down just over a year ago, when the Liberal government in Halifax was being assisted by the Liberal government in Ottawa. We now have a Conservative government in Halifax and we have a Conservative government in Ottawa, and those governments are working in cooperation with each other and are accomplishing something for the coal industry.
I deprecate the pessimism which has been exhibited in this house. This afternoon my hon. friend went off the course. He did not have much to say about the coal industry, so he became Jeremiah and wrote the third book of Jeremiah when he talked about the closing of all the industries in Nova Scotia. Although I was sure he was sincerely sorry to have to enumerate the long list of shut downs, one could not but detect a slight gleam in his eye. He went on to speak of the Moirs woodworking company which had been closed down and he also mentioned several plants

which had been closed down, burned down, or had gone out of operation in the last ten years.
What was the Liberal coal policy? We have heard a great deal said about that and certainly the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) and the hon. member for In-verness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan), who spoke yesterday afternoon referred to it. I do not have to recap or recount the coal policy of the former government but perhaps, just to keep the record straight-having in mind that this was referred to by the hon. member who has just sat down-I should say that their so-called coal policy did not come anywhere near meeting our problems. The people of Nova Scotia refused to accept it and the Liberal government itself did not know just what it was. They talked about producing coal at cost and using it for producing power. As the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond said, "What is cost?" It could be anything.
This government, before the election of June 10, laid down its policy. We said if we were elected we would build thermal plants which would produce electricity cheaper than it was then being produced. That was our pledge, and that pledge has been kept. We have inaugurated a policy as a result of which we expect and believe that thermal power will be developed in Nova Scotia at a comparable cost to that of power in Ontario at the present time. This is really a major gain.
Our interests were twofold; (a) to promote the coal industry in Nova Scotia and (b) to promote the natural development of our province. We tried to do these two things together, using our coal industry and development of our power, and by means of subventions are bringing down the cost of the power produced in that area.
This is the program we have been carrying out and which we are carrying out today. There has been a great deal of complaint, and particularly complaint about some plant to be built in Saint John-whether it is going to use coal or whether it is not going to use coal. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the magnificent speech he made yesterday afternoon pointed out that no one could foresee the future for generations or even for years to come. But this can be said without any question whatsoever,-namely that any thermal plant receiving assistance from the federal government today, tomorrow or in the reasonably foreseeable future, is going to burn Nova Scotia or maritime coal or it will not get subventions. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate last night said he wanted a statement on that subject, and I hope this

Would the minister permit a question? Would he state whether that stipulation will be put into the contract for the Saint John plant, as Mr. Stanfield said it would?
I am not discussing contracts at the moment.
No; exactly.
Oh, oh.

Will you stop that "ah-hah". That is about all you know. Some of you are used to the kind of government which thinks everything has to be in black and white and that everything has to be written in a contract if commitments are not to be broken.

The government's policy was that the power should be developed. The Liberals, then the government, in a last dying effort produced the so-called Winters scheme for the development of power, and the merit of that can be judged by the fact that last night the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate admitted that it was on June 6, in the dying days of a dying campaign of a dying government that the government made a commitment with respect to using coal in the Nova Scotia thermal power plants.

Coal

Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines *
After they had kicked us in the teeth for years.

That is the merit of the so-called program advanced. We advanced our own program. It was accepted by the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in June; it was accepted again this March. It is being carried out, and it will be carried out; and, as I said a few moments ago, coal will be used in all plants which have received subventions or assistance from this government for the reasonably foreseeable future. Here again, look at the difference between the two schemes. These plants are going to be operated by the provincial governments, under provincial control.
One could go on and on, but I think I have said enough to suggest that the record of this government with respect to its coal policy, and the increased assistance which we have given to the industry during the short time we have been in office, have re-established the faith of the people with respect to putting the industry on a firm basis again and the people of Nova Scotia have no doubt as to where this government stands with respect to it. I say this because never before has any government gone so far as we have gone in co-operation with the provincial government in extending this subvention.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say, what about next year? I do not know about next year. Next year is another year. We are dealing with the present. We have made arrangements to provide full employment for the miners in the mine fields of Nova Scotia operated by the company subject to the 25-day lay-off which the company, as I explained before, said was inevitable and which they intended to carry out in any event.
It may be that next year again the -coal industry will face -difficulties. I do not know. If it does, I think this government has shown its interest in the coal industry in the province, so it would be prepared to give consideration to the problem if it should again arise. This action taken by the government the other day has both negative and positive implications. It is negative in that it prevented a lay-off. To that extent it is negative, although even this was very positive to the people who are not to be laid off. But it also has a positive implication, because the government would not have achieved this temporary result if they had thought that in a few months time the effort would be abortive and useless.
The government believe that the future of the Nova Scotia coal industry can be reestablished and is reasonably bright. We have seen an example within the last few


days, when the Ontario hydro commission chairman said that within a year or two he would be buying well over one million tons of coal and that within 10 years, even after making allowances for the St. Lawrence seaway and all the other developments of hydro electric power-he, or rather the hydro commission, would be buying over 10 million tons of coal according to the present expansion program for Ontario.
All it comes to, Mr. Speaker, is a redirection of this subvention, a little here and a little there. We have already broken into Ontario to a fairly substantial degree, and by increasing subventions, which might not necessitate an over-all increase at all, you could move Nova Scotia coal into this tremendous market which is so very near and capable of so much expansion, this market which is going to develop along the seaway. And with the development of the seaway both ways, United States coal may come down, but Nova Scotia coal can go up.
I remember when I was sitting on the other side of the house I quoted from dominion coal board figures which said that by 1965 the coal industry, not only of Nova Scotia but the -coal industry generally, would be on the upsurge again because of increasing costs of producing oil and other fuels. And I believed what I said when I said that the future of the industry is bright.
We have a new -company. It must be remembered that the company only took over last November; it has not -been there very long, but the management has been aggressive and intelligent in developing new sales policies; and with the collaboration of the governments and that management I believe that within a relatively short period, a year or two at the outset, we could develop a market for Nova Scotia coal, and develop the production of Nova Scotia coal.
One thing which I believe to be really bad about this lay-off is not the financial loss so much but the fact that the miners who have worked so hard might feel that if they had not worked quite so hard they would not be facing a lay-off. I hope the leaders of the industry will avoid that mistake being made, because we have to have continual production and continual effort, the co-operation of management and labour in the industry, and given those things we can solve this problem and we will do so.
In so far as this specific amendment is concerned, we are told first that the house regrets that the government has failed to avert a five-week shut-down. As I said a moment ago, it is true there is to be a five-week shut-down. But we did not fail to avert

it, because the company said it was inevitable in any event. When they came before us with this proposition they had already announced the five-week shut-down as something which they, or any company in a similar position, would be bound to institute.
Then the amendment expresses regret that the government has backed away from its commitment to promote the establishment of industry in the Atlantic provinces. That is absolutely fallacious and without any foundation in fact or fancy. The policy of this government is twofold. As I said, it is to help promote the coal mines, to develop cheaper power, and to develop industry. And in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island industry depends on power and transportation. We have taken the steps necessary to provide cheaper power and to avert an increase in freight rates not only in the maritimes but elsewhere in Canada, and we are going to take other steps with regard to transportation problems in the maritimes and in the rest of Canada. This government will, I am confident, have shown before very long that it is responsible for a tremendous development of industry in the maritimes as well as in Canada generally.
The last part of the amendment reads:
And particularly from its specific undertaking to ensure the use of coal in thermal plants assisted financially by the federal government.
That again is a sheer figment of the imagination. The government has not departed from the policy announced by the Prime Minister that we are going to insist that all thermal plants in the maritime provinces receiving federal assistance shall burn coal. That is our policy. It has been stated by the Prime Minister, and it is beyond challenge and contradiction.
I do not think there is any point in commenting further on the statements that have been made. As I said earlier, the speeches that were made by hon. members yesterday were speeches of which I was proud as a minister coming from Nova Scotia. They were speeches of which I am sure all hon. members of this side of the house and the people of Nova Scotia in general will be proud as well when they read reports of them in today's newspapers. The speeches were a credit to this house and to those who made them. Hon. members who entered into the debate come from coal constituencies in which they have a lifetime of personal knowledge and experience, and it was rewarding to see the keen interest they took in the matter.
Under the circumstances I suggest that the house cannot possibly accept the amendment

Coal-Shutdown of Nova Scotia Mines which has been proposed and I urge that it be defeated when it is brought to a vote this evening.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to have the privilege of saying a few words on this amendment though I have to confess that perhaps in the eyes of the hon. minister who just sat down I am disqualified from doing so because I am an ex-professor.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when we reached six o'clock I was attempting to deal with the remarks which have been made on the amendment before the house by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and had suggested that those remarks would be found, in some respects at least, to be quite inconsistent with what was said by his colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) last evening. Before I proceed to point out that inconsistency I had better put on the record very briefly, because there is not much time available, Liberal policy in respect of the particular question which is dealt with in the amendment.
As hon. members must know, Liberal policy was to apply subventions to make coal competitive with oil in thermal power plants in the Atlantic provinces, which we thought and still think was the best way, not only to help the coal industry but to bring about the cheapest possible production of power in those areas where cheap power is certainly needed. Indeed, it was our intention to assist in the production of power so that it could be distributed at cost.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I must say I was very interested indeed in one remark made by the Minister of National Revenue on this particular point of distributing products at cost of production. In the 25 years that I have had the honour of being an elected member either of federal or provincial parliaments I believe I have earned the reputation of being an extemporaneous speaker. In 25 years I have never used comprehensive notes. However, Mr. Speaker, with your permission, and with the forbearance of hon. members, I intend to do so this evening in order to try to put forward every aspect of an important grievance.
What we have in mind is a problem which afflicts very seriously an important sector of the Canadian economy, namely the small business group. May I first of all emphasize that we in the C.C.F. have always recognized the indispensable role which small business plays in the Canadian economy. I know I am safe in saying that without our service industries, without our retail and other distributed outlets, without our small production industries, our communities in Canada would find it almost impossible to produce and to distribute effectively the nation's commercial and industrial products. I am certain all hon. members will agree that our service industries, which, of necessity, include many small businesses, are, have been, and will be an integral part of our complex economic organization.
Our group has given a great deal of thought over many weeks and months to the position of small business in Canada, and we fail to understand, in view of the importance of small business and small industries to our economy, why there has as yet been no development policy brought forward, no adequate program which would meet the particular difficulty of small business and small industries, namely the problem of long term financing. I feel quite certain that many members of this house know that a great many small businesses in Canada have long been confronted with the difficulty of raising long term credit in order to finance their capital requirements, and it is on this particular phase of small business that we desire to speak at this time.
I think all hon. members will agree that if a small business is properly managed then it has access to the chartered banks but as a general rule small business can only obtain a short term loan from a chartered bank. That is understandable because it has been the traditional practice with only one or two special exceptions for the chartered banks to 57071-3-1154
Small Business-Long term Credit limit their lending to short term credit. Small and medium-sized businesses are dependent upon banks for short term credit and as a general rule these loans do not extend over a year. Indeed, in the majority of cases the loans are repaid inside of a year. On the other hand long term lending has generally been shunned by the banks in our country and that too is understandable because it is based on the nature of our banking system which is deposit banking. Since deposits in banks are withdrawable either on demand or on very short notice the banking institutions of this country have understandably maintained the policy of keeping their assets comparatively liquid. I think it is because of that need that they have not in the past extended long term loans to small business and to small industry. However, there is a great need for such loans to be extended to small business and industry.
I am certain that hon. members will remember that there were some bankers who were opposed to the National Housing Act of 1954 which allowed the banks to enter the long-term mortgage field. Experience since 1954, however, has clearly demonstrated that banks can allocate a certain amount of their bank credit in the form of long term mortgage loans without impairing to any appreciable degree what is termed the liquidity of the position of the banks. The logical course for a large firm that wants a long-term loan is to raise money either by floating a stock issue or, if it wants to raise non-equity capital, by selling a bond or debenture issue, but this is not possible for small industry or small business.
All hon. members, I am sure, will accept as axiomatic that a small firm or industry would have little hope of being able to raise the necessary capital funds by going to an investment house, a brokerage firm or an insurance company in an effort to raise money through the issuance of debentures. The position of the banks in the past, as I have said, is definitely understandable but I think we must also recognize that small industry and small business are on the horns of a dilemma. They cannot obtain long term loans from the banks and neither can they go through the medium available to large business to raise required capital.
If hon. members will only think back a little I feel certain they will remember that a gap in the financial structure of this country was filled in 1944 by the establishment of the industrial development bank. The primary purpose of this public corporation was to supply long term capital to small and medium-sized businesses which, for the reasons I have already mentioned, could not

Small Business-Long term Credit obtain such capital from the private financial institutions. The bank was empowered to lend money or guarantee loans made by private credit institutions or even to acquire common stock, bonds or debentures from the issuing corporation with which it had entered into an underwriting agreement. While the industrial development bank has helped to fill the gap its operations have been limited, as its name implies, to assisting industrial enterprises. Not even the changes in the act made in 1956 which somewhat broadened the field of eligible businesses have substantially changed the situation. Consequently there are still many small businesses which do not qualify under the lending terms of this bank. We feel that some action must be taken to assist small industry and business.
Several important questions come to mind when we consider a plan or policy to meet this situation but we in this group remind hon. members first of all of the principles underlying the industrial development bank and also of the changes that were made only a short time ago in the National Housing Act to permit for the first time the chartered banks of Canada to enter the long term lending mortgage field. I believe I am correct in saying that the banks have in no way retreated from their position of liquidity because of their entering this field. Presumably guarantees could be extended to the chartered banking system in the field of loans to qualifying small industry and business if the government would only set its mind to tackling this most important problem.
We say that experience in Canada has definitely proved that bank credit if used wisely can be employed up to a point in financing long term requirements. Because of the experience of the industrial development bank, the chartered banks and the wonderful facilities offered by the chartered banks with all their branches throughout Canada, we suggest to the house and the government a plan to aid small industry and small business to obtain the required capital on a reasonable long term basis.

Our group recommends to the consideration of the house a five point program which I should like to enumerate at this time. We suggest the following program:
1. Broaden the class of loans under the industrial development bank to include a broad coverage of non-industrial enterprises such as the service industries, distributive trades, etc.

2.	Increase the capitalization of the industrial development bank to accommodate increased lending, investing and guaranteeing of loans.
3.	Amend the Bank Act to allow chartered banks to lend money or make advances to qualifying small business upon the security, mortgage or hypothecation of real or immovable property. May I say that this would be in addition to the special exceptions which have already been made in this respect under the National Housing Act, 1954, and the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
4.	Guarantee term loans by chartered banks to small business against losses up to 10 per cent of the total amount of such loans made by any bank. May I add there that the figure of 10 per cent was chosen by our group because the same percentage is operative under similar guarantees, for example, with respect to farm improvement loans.
5.	Enable chartered banks to sell mortgages securing such term loans to the industrial development bank in the same way in which the banks are enabled to sell housing mortgages to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Furthermore, ensure that banks can receive advances from the Bank of Canada using such mortgages as eligible security in the same way in which they can receive advances from the Bank of Canada using housing mortgages as security.
We in this group, Mr. Speaker, feel that not only is such a plan necessary in Canada at this time but that it is feasible, practical and will assist small business and industry. It will protect the banks making the loans because it puts them in the same position as they are at the present time with respect to long term advances for housing or farm loans. We propose this program with the object of opening up a new avenue by which the chartered banks, working in close-cooperation with a revised industrial development bank, could grant capital assistance in the form of term loans to qualifying small businesses. To some it may seem a novel approach but it is no more novel than the legislation passed by the house in 1954 which allowed the banks, for the first time in their history, to go into the mortgage lending field under the National Housing Act. In order to guarantee what is termed the liquidity of the banks and thus maintain the complete integrity of deposit banking the necessary safeguards have been provided in the five points I have outlined on behalf of this group.
We believe that the program we are proposing at this time will fill a gap in the financial structure of the country, a gap

which has long handicapped small business. We hope that it will receive the most serious consideration by members of the house and the most serious consideration of the government which would have to bring in the required legislation.

I should like to mention a few figures and statistics in order to point out the necessity of instituting such a program as that proposed by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East. This statistical information comes from the dominion bureau of statistics publication on commercial failures under the Bankruptcy and Winding-Up Acts. With reference to the number of business failures or insolvencies over the past few years we find there has been a gradual increase in the number. To compare last year with the year before, according to the statistics we find that there was an increase of some 12 per cent in the number of failures and an increase numerically from 1,967 to 2,198. I might add that of those 2,198 insolvencies last year, 1,320 of them involved wage earners and lost wages where people did not get their wages because the company had gone bankrupt. The others that did not involve loss of wages were wholly-owned or family-owned businesses. The amount of total liabilities over 1956 also increased by some 9 per cent.
But the most interesting point in the application of these statistics to the proposal made by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East is the average amount of liabilities incurred by the businesses which went insolvent. Last year the average amount was $31,900, which was certainly not a large amount of money compared with the indebtedness and liabilities that might be incurred if some of our multi-million dollar corporations in Canada went bankrupt. I might point out that 57 per cent of the entire number of insolvencies were ones having liabilities in the bracket between $5,000 and $25,000 while over 86 per cent were ones having liabilities of less than $50,000. This is in the field of being a small business in terms of liabilities and in terms of money.
If we had legislation that would allow businesses as those to which I have just referred the opportunity of participating in the

While there are many more, some of the particular types of small business which are referred to in this statistical information are filling stations, clothing stores, furniture stores, radio and appliance shops, food stores, general merchants, drug stores and the like which are similar to the small corner grocery store type business. All for the lack of a few dollars they find themselves in difficulties. I am sure many of these businesses could have been saved, could have been put on their feet, could have been contributing to the economy of Canada and could have been employing a few more of the wage earners of the country.
As everyone knows, in our so-called free enterprise system-which as many know is not a free enterprise system at all-these small businesses particularly have a most difficult time in competing against the huge monopoly corporations that we have. They are just not in the same class at all. A review of the various inquiries made under the Combines Investigation Act will show that a small concern attempting to buck a large group of chain stores or a large monopoly corporation or semi-monopoly corporation has a most difficult time in doing so and can easily be wiped out of business if the large concern so desires and puts its mind to it. In fact that has happened in the past on many occasions.
If there is any thought of attempting to advance the philosophy of free enterprise as it was originally evolved and not as we have it at the present time, then we must enter into some relationship like this in order to protect the smaller concerns-these people who are in effect no nearer being a capitalist than I am-the businesses which are in effect merely in the working class group but which try to participate in society and try to find a means of expressing themselves through the type of business that they develop or start. If there is any thought at all in the minds of those on the government benches opposite of establishing some protection for these small business people against the effect that monopoly enterprise has on them at the present time, here is an opportunity to move in that direction and to establish such legislation so

He went on, however, to set out a five point platform on behalf of the C.C.F. group designed to broaden the class of loans under the industrial development bank, to increase the capitalization of the industrial development bank, to amend the Bank Act in order to allow them to make loans upon mortgages or hypothecations in addition to the provisions of the National Housing Act, to guarantee term loans made by banks to small businesses and to enable the chartered banks to sell mortgage securities.

The hon. member for Vancouver East went into great detail about some of the problems of small businesses, of which I am well aware, and some of which apply to my own constituency, but our government has gone ahead and has made provision for the setting up of a committee to study these problems. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) with regard to the proposals made by my colleague from Vancouver East. Though expressing a great deal of appreciation and understanding of the problems of small business, he seemed to feel that the suggestions put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East were possibly conceived in some haste. I should like at once to assure the hon. member that this problem of the small businessman has been considered at considerable length by the C.C.F. movement for a goodly number of years. We realize the seriousness of the problem and its far-reaching implications for the Canadian consumer, to an extent that we have had a continuing committee studying this matter for many years.
The hon. member seemed interested in knowing where the headquarters of small business are to be found in Canada. I know he comes from the city of Winnipeg. I have before me here a letterhead from, I assume, the secretariat of the retail merchants association of Canada, and I can tell the hon. member that the head office is in his city of Winnipeg. As for the idea proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver East being, in the main, so unique or novel, may I offer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre a suggestion that it is nothing of the kind.
I should like to read this submission of the retail merchants association of Canada as made in a letter to me dated April 13, 1957. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will then see a very close similarity to the proposals put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East when he spoke on behalf of this group with regard to this grievance. The submission says, on page 2:
This association has made the suggestion that a Retail Business Capital Loans Act be set up for the purpose of enabling retailers to borrow money for rehabilitation and expansion. We have suggested that the mechanics of such an act be similar to those of the Homes Improvement Loans Act, i.e., that the individual loans be made through the chartered banks, with a government guarantee.
This could be done by authorizing the bank to advance 50 to 75 per cent of the cost of the proposed improvement or extension of buildings, equipment, parking facilities, etc. The loans would be repayable over a period of years. As we pointed out previously, such a plan would not introduce any new principle into Canadian finance. Similar assistance has already been extended to fishermen, farmers, manufacturers, home-owners and home repairs, food processors, etc.
So the idea has been given serious thought over a long period of years. With the assumption of office by this new government we had thought that some action would be forthcoming during this session. The Minister of

Justice (Mr. Fulton) indicated, after the speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, that the hon. member had obviously not read the speech from the throne. I think the grievance remains a grievance despite anything I read in the speech from the throne. The speech from the throne is somewhat along the lines of the proposal made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in that it predicts that a committee or a branch of a department of government will be set up to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them. We feel that the small businessmen of Canada were given an assurance that their problem had been considered and that the necessary action would be forthcoming. There is such a thing as chickens coming home to roost, and the various promises that have been made by the Conservative party are coming home to roost now with great and growing rapidity, and these chickens are rather blue. They are bluer than the Tory party, and they are coming thick and fast.
I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) endorse the activities of the industrial development bank and, as the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) pointed out, it stands to the credit of the Liberal party that this bank was established and has been so influential in assisting individual enterprises in Canada.
The C.C.F. party has always in this house been a strong supporter of the industrial development bank, and in effect all we are asking now is that its powers be broadened so as to enable it to render a service to the small businessman.
Some argument has arisen in debating this grievance as to what constitutes a small business. My interpretation of a small business in need of government interest and concern is a business not necessarily of a certain size or volume with regard to its assets, but a business in which there is some relationship between ownership and management. It may be a business consisting of $5,000 or $10,000 of assets; it may go as high as half a million dollars depending on the type of enterprise. I think our society has lost something by divorcing management from ownership, and that those engaged in business have a little less chance to be responsible members of our society now that this separation of ownership and management is taking place.
The record of our group in speaking on behalf of the individual in Canada is very clear indeed. The very reason for our being

in existence as a political force is that we feel that with the way things are going at the present time the rights of the individual are disappearing day by day in our society. The tendency of big business to consolidate and amalgamate robs the individual engaged as an employee in enterprise of a large share of his individualism. Eventually he finds he has become a mere cog in a machine. His position is different from that of a civil servant who renders a service to society as a whole. That is different and distinct from the relationship of the individual working in a huge enterprise who does little more than punch a machine or go through a certain routine. This party has always supported genuine free enterprise. In fact, the birth of this political party came about through the growing power of monopolistic corporations and their influence on the individuals in our nation.
I am assuming that the present grievance is that this government is not taking action to help small business in Canada. This was demonstrated when the government did not express any sympathy for the idea of placing a limitation on interest rates. Huge department stores through their financing methods are able to squeeze the small businessman to the wall. This applies particularly in the appliance field where these huge corporations do not care how much net profit they make on the sale of an article because they make their net earnings on the finance charges they are allowed to levy. If the Tory party believes in competition to the extent it professes it might very well reconsider its position with regard to placing a limitation on finance charges. This would be a valuable way of giving assistance to the small enterpriser and the small merchant in Canada.
Another device that might be used would be to make more effective the anti-combines legislation of this country. The practices of combines tend to gobble up free enterprise in one field after another on the Canadian scene.
Another cause of the hardship of the small businessman is that he is not able to buy on the same terms as is the large business enterpriser. I feel that an amendment to the combines legislation might serve an extremely useful purpose so that when a small corner store orders one case of Lifebuoy soap the owner will not be charged a higher price than is charged a huge chain store for the same product. In view of the huge overhead paid by large businesses and especially by chain stores I am convinced that small merchants would be able to compete very successfully with them if they were able to buy at the same price levels.
